intro.html: English has many words for destroying, and each one paints a slightly different picture: knocking down, laying waste, pulling up by the roots, wiping out every letter, or taking apart piece by piece.
Knocking down buildings: demolish, raze. Wide damage: devastate, ravage, decimate (a large part). Wiping out every trace: eradicate, annihilate, obliterate, expunge. Taking apart: dismantle.
Many of these words carry Latin pictures: eradicate holds radix (root), annihilate holds nihil (nothing), obliterate holds littera (letter), and decimate holds decimus (tenth).

words.def: to knock down or destroy completely
words.ex: The crew will {demolish} the old warehouse to make room for a park.
words.ctx: The debate champion did more than disagree with her opponent’s claim; she {demolished} it, showing that every one of his facts was wrong.
words.etym: From Latin demoliri, “to tear down”: de- (down) + moliri (to build, to heave a great mass).

mn.text: Theo spends one second looking at his sister’s tall block tower, then knocks the whole thing flat; he can {demolish} it faster than anyone can build it.

scene.alt: A laughing toddler knocks down a tall tower of blocks while his sister gasps.

words.def: to destroy over a wide area; also, to overwhelm with grief or shock
words.ex: The hailstorm {devastated} the farmer’s whole field of corn.
words.ctx: The news {devastated} the team; after a season of hard work, they had been knocked out of the tournament because of a mistake on a single form.

roots.means: to make, to act on (in verbs)

words.etym: From Latin devastare, “to lay waste”: de- (completely) + vastare (to lay waste), from vastus (empty, vast).

mn.cue: DE-VAST-ATE: a VAST field laid waste
mn.text: A storm flattens a vast field of sunflowers in a single night, and the farmer drops to her knees; the storm has {devastated} her farm.

scene.alt: A farmer kneels in tears as a storm flattens her field of flowers.

words.ex: Locusts {ravaged} the valley, stripping every field bare.
words.ctx: The wildfire {ravaged} the hills for a week, leaving blackened trunks where green forest had stood.
words.etym: From French ravager, from ravir (to seize, to carry off).
words.note: The plural noun ravages means heavy damage: the ravages of time, the ravages of war.

mn.text: A herd of ravenous goats storms through Granny Mae’s garden and leaves nothing but stalks and torn petals; they {ravage} it.

scene.alt: Two goats tear through a garden, scattering leaves and flowers, as a grandmother cries out.

words.def: to wipe out completely, as if pulling up by the roots
words.ex: The town worked for years to {eradicate} the weeds choking the pond.
words.ctx: Health workers set out to {eradicate} the disease entirely, vaccinating children in every village until not a single new case was reported.

roots.means: to make, to act on (in verbs)

words.etym: From Latin eradicare, “to pull out by the roots”: e- (out) + radix (root). Radish comes from radix too.

mn.text: Grandpa Gus does not just snip the weed; he yanks it out by the roots like a radish so it can never grow back. He wants to {eradicate} it.

scene.alt: A grandfather leans back and yanks a weed out of the ground, roots and all.

words.def: to destroy completely; also, to defeat by a huge margin
words.ex: In the board game final, Maya {annihilated} her brothers, winning by four hundred points.
words.ctx: The volcano’s eruption {annihilated} the island’s forest; where thousands of trees had stood, there was nothing but gray ash.

roots.means: to make, to act on (in verbs)

words.etym: From Late Latin annihilare, “to bring to nothing”: ad- (to) + nihil (nothing).

mn.text: Zoe wins the checkers final 400 to nil; her brother is left with nothing at all. She {annihilates} him.

scene.alt: A girl cheers beside a scoreboard reading 400 to 0 while her brother covers his eyes.

words.def: to wipe out so completely that no trace is left
words.ex: The tide {obliterated} the names we had written in the sand.
words.ctx: Years of wind and rain had {obliterated} the painted letters on the old barn, so no one remembered what the farm had once been called.

roots.means: to make, to act on (in verbs)

words.etym: From Latin obliterare, “to blot out, to make forgotten”: ob- (against) + littera (letter).

mn.text: Lila writes her name in huge letters on the sand, and one big wave wipes out every letter until no trace is left; the wave {obliterates} it.

scene.alt: A wave washes over a girl’s name written in the sand, wiping out the letters.

words.def: to destroy a large part of something
words.ex: A harsh winter {decimated} the deer herd, leaving only a few dozen animals.
words.ctx: The new highway {decimated} the little town’s business: with drivers speeding past, most of its diners and gas stations closed within two years.

roots.means: to make, to act on (in verbs)

words.etym: From Latin decimare, from decimus (tenth). It first named a harsh Roman army punishment that struck one soldier in every ten.

mn.cue: DECI = TEN, but now MOST are gone
mn.text: Nell baked a hundred cookies; while she answered the door, the dog ate all but ten. He {decimated} the batch.

scene.alt: A happy dog sits by a nearly empty cookie plate while the baker cries out.

words.def: to tear down completely, all the way to the ground
words.ex: The city plans to {raze} the crumbling old mill next spring.
words.ctx: Rather than repair the leaning barn, the farmers decided to {raze} it; by evening nothing was left but a flat patch of dirt where it had stood.
words.etym: From older English rase, “to scrape, to shave off.”
words.note: Raze sounds just like raise, but the two are opposites: to raise a barn is to build it; to raze it is to tear it down.

mn.cue: RAZE is the opposite of RAISE
mn.text: On one lot the crew raises a new house; on the next lot they tear the old one flat. To {raze} a building is the opposite of raising it.

scene.alt: On one side a builder stands by a new house; on the other, an old building lies flattened in a cloud of dust.

words.ex: Once the mistake was found, the school {expunged} the late mark from her record.
words.ctx: The judge agreed to {expunge} the old charge from his record, so it would no longer appear when employers checked his background.
words.etym: From Latin expungere, “to mark for deletion with dots”: ex- (out) + pungere (to prick).

mn.text: Coach Omar takes a big wet sponge and wipes Kai’s name off the list of late players; the mark is gone, {expunged}.

scene.alt: A coach wipes a boy’s name off the late list with a sponge while the boy cheers.

words.def: to take apart piece by piece
words.ex: Dad had to {dismantle} the bunk bed to get it through the doorway.
words.ctx: Rather than repair the broken clock, the curious student {dismantled} it, laying every gear and spring on the table in neat rows.
words.etym: From Middle French desmanteler, “to strip of a cloak,” and so of a fort’s walls: des- (away) + mantel (cloak).

mn.cue: DIS-MAN-TLE: the robot MAN in pieces
mn.text: Sami unscrews the old robot man bolt by bolt and lines every piece up on the floor; he {dismantles} it to see how it works.

scene.alt: A boy in goggles kneels with a wrench, taking a robot apart and lining up its gears.

after.cap: Ten ways to destroy, and what each leaves behind.

after.html: Decimate once meant destroying exactly one in ten; today it means destroying a large part, but not all. If everything is gone, choose annihilate or obliterate.

items.q: True or false: to raze a building means to put it up.
items.why: False. Raze means to tear down to the ground. It sounds like raise, its opposite.

items.q: “The storm decimated the orchard.” Most careful readers take this to mean the storm…
choices: destroyed a large part of it
items.why: Decimate once meant to destroy one in ten; today it means to destroy a large part.
radix means root (as in radish): to eradicate is to pull something out by the roots.

items.q: Which word means to take apart piece by piece, not to smash?
items.why: To dismantle is to take something apart carefully. The other words mean destroying.
